newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish GDP seen up 6.1 pct despite flood-institute.
newsitem.headline: Polish GDP seen up 6.1 pct despite flood-institute.

text.p: Poland's gross domestic product (GDP) soared 8.2 percent in the second quarter and should grow by 6.1 percent in the whole of 1997 despite a third quarter slow-down due to heavy floods, an independent think-tank said.
The Gdansk-based Market Economic Reseach Institute (IBnGR) said year-on-year GDP growth would slow to 3.1 percent in the third quarter before rising to six percent in the last quarter.

"In the second quarter of the year we have witnessed the fastest economic growth Poland has seen since the start of economic transformation seven years ago," Miroslaw Gronicki, chief analyst at IBnGR, told a news conference on Thursday.
Poland's 1997 budget envisioned GDP growth at 5.5 percent after a 6.1 percent rise in 1996.
"The economy is definitely overheating with domestic demand growing faster than output and facilitating a quick widening of the current account and trade deficits," Gronicki added.

Despite this Gronicki was confident that Poland's trade gap would stay capped in 1998 after reaching some $13 billion this year if the zloty remains weak, credit rates continue to grow in real terms and the budget deficit was lowered as planned.

"The central bank has to up market rates, which has already begun, but it does not have to increase official interest rates to sufficiently cool domestic demand...if next year's budget deficit is cut to the planned 1.9 percent of GDP," he said.
He said the zloty should stabilise two to three percent below the parity rate in the medium term and a reduction in the present one percent per month crawling peg devaluation was unlikely in 1997.

"A tighter central bank monetary policy and lower budget gap could consolidate the Polish economy next year but at the cost of economic growth -- which could slow to about 4.7 percent in 1998," Gronicki said.
He said an additional flood tax should be introduced to help rebuild damaged flood areas without putting more strain on the budget, which could experience more difficulties in 1997.

"There are likely to be budget tensions this year despite the increased ability for the government to borrow from the central bank as various budgetary reserves were funneled into flood relief," he said.

He said the additional monetary outflow triggered by the relief effort, along with fast growth of Poland's currency reserves in the second quarter, may push price growth above the year-on-year 13 percent inflation target in December.

"The potential for meeting the (13-percent) target is not as high now as it was a month ago, before the floods...but the average inflation rate in the fourth quarter should still fall to about 14 percent," Gronicki said.
IBnGR said average inflation in the second quarter was 15.1 percent and that it would fall to 14.3 percent in the third.

He said Poland's current account should be helped by a weaker zloty over the next year or more and a pickup in cross-border trade inflows, which rose in the second quarter of 1997 after falling by one-third in the first quarter against first quarter 1996.

Gronicki said that if credit rates remain high and consumer demand was cooled, the structure of imports could slant further toward investment or infrastructure goods as the giant flood relief effort gets underway.
